description: We are developing a space exploration and survival game inspired by real astronomy and NASA data. Players will experience life as astronauts, explore space environments, manage resources, and overcome challenges using realistic physics. By combining real astronomical images, image processing, scientific data, and immersive storytelling, our project aims to turn space science into an interactive adventure that makes exploring the universe both exciting and educational.
summary: The Last Known Signal is a Unity game that teaches how real space missions are designed. A relay satellite has gone silent and the player, working from a NASA-style mission base, must design and fly a rescue. In Design Mode and the Planner, the player balances ship mass, redundancy, power and mission days against the limits of a real launch vehicle (NASA's Space Launch System). Then they fly through missions where real NASA data creates the challenges: solar flares and coronal mass ejections, close approaches of near-Earth asteroids, radio signal delay, falling sunlight at distance, and a rocky exoplanet (TRAPPIST-1 e). Every debrief shows the NASA source behind what just happened. It addresses the Space Mission Design Game challenge by letting players experience the trade-offs mission designers face, which makes space-mission engineering understandable to students and the public.
details:
Main use. A player-facing way to learn mission design trade-offs: a heavier ship is safer but harder to launch, and every extra system costs power and mass. The result is a "planned success" figure that changes with the player's choices and with events during the mission.

What it does (built, from the project log)

A story campaign of missions (M1 and M2 ground tests and launch preparation, M3 deep-space flight, M4 landing on a rocky exoplanet, a final call-home scene) with a risk gauge, a father's-log story, and a mascot guide named Pip.

A reusable Planner where the player trades part grade and redundancy against a mass budget, with a live resource box (power, mission days, launch vehicle) and a 5-step skippable tutorial.

Design Mode with destinations, a build screen, a launch-vehicle picker (SLS Block 1, 1B, Block 2) and a lift check that blocks launch with a stated reason if the ship is too heavy.

M3 free 3D flight with floating origin and no soft-locks, and four challenge sites. Each site opens a NASA DATA card (dataset, source link, why NASA cares, real values), offers three choices with costs, and changes the player's supplies, hull, power and planned success. A seeded random picks the site order, so runs differ.

Flight visuals: Earth, Moon and Sun, solar-flare bursts, asteroid close-pass warnings, a comms beam with visible light delay, eclipse dimming.

A skippable opening scene of about 38 seconds, and subtitled narration with 43 voice clips.

A DATA & SOURCES screen, a NASA DATA block on every debrief, and an end card listing the datasets that shaped the run.

Verification so far: 87 automated EditMode tests (86 pass, 1 explicit skip) and a Windows player build that succeeded with a smoke run that logged no errors.

How it works. Game data is loaded from CSV files in the project. Each file has a source link and retrieval date, and every dataset is registered in data_sources.csv. The risk model combines the player's plan with event outcomes into a success probability. Choices carry costs; each scenario has a free fallback option so the game never soft-locks.

Tools. Unity 6000.6.9f1 with the Universal Render Pipeline, C#, HLSL shaders, Blender and Node.js scripts for models, Piper text-to-speech for narration, Git. Language of the game and all content: English.

Limitations

NASA data is a snapshot retrieved on 2026-11-13 and 2026-11-14, not live.

Reliabilities, subsystem masses, mass budgets, supply days, mission days and event costs are game-balance values, not NASA data, and are tagged on screen.

In M3 the Mars and Moon rows from Horizons are story stand-ins for the ship and the relay; the Mars-to-Moon distance is derived and labelled so. Solar flux is derived from the inverse-square law and labelled so.

Event scenarios use real values but the situations themselves are fictional.

Narration is synthetic placeholder-quality voice.

A full human play-through, a frame-rate check, and a human re-check of each NASA source link were still pending when this was written. ⟦update once done⟧

Windows only.

Future plans

Live data feeds instead of snapshots.

More missions and destinations, human-voiced narration, other platforms.
